questions_and_answers.question_text: What two ways may jiā be used?
What does the general object shū really mean?
Whose children are sūnzi and sūnnǚ?
What are the children of one's daughter called?
Write the Chinese for "Everyone in that family works."
How is niànguo bù shǎo shū best translated?

answers.answer_text: "To be very well educated" or "to have a good education."

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which two of the Four Books were chapters of the Book of Rites?

answers.answer_text: Dàxué ("The Great Learning") and Zhōngyōng ("The Doctrine of the Mean").

questions_and_answers.question_text: Who raised them to the status of separate books?

answers.answer_text: The Southern Sòng Dynasty philosopher Zhū Xī.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Did many older Chinese study the Four Books?

answers.answer_text: Yes — many older Chinese you meet today studied them as children.

articles.text:
7. A: Zhèi yìjiā rén dōu niànguo    This whole family has had quite a
      bù shǎo shū.                  good education.
   B: Tīngshuō tāmende sūnzi       I understand that their grandsons and
      sūnnǚ xiànzài dōu niàn Sì     granddaughters are all studying the
      Shū ne!                       Four Books now!

Notes on No. 7

Zhèi yìjiā rén: "this family." You already know that jiā can be used as a NOUN meaning "family." But jiā can also be used as a COUNTER. It may be used alone or with the noun rén following.

Nèi yìjiā, rénrén dōu gōngzuò.   Everyone in that family works.
Cóng zhèi sānjiā rénde qíngxing, From the situations of these three
nǐ kěyi zhīdao yìxiē guānyú      families, you can learn something
Zhōngguo rénde shēnghuó.         about the life of the Chinese.

niànguo bù shǎo shū: Literally, "studied a lot of books." This is the GENERAL OBJECT shū. It doesn't really mean "books," but ANYTHING AT ALL which is studied. Niàn shū just means "to study, to be in school," so we translate niànguo bù shǎo shū as "to be very well educated."

Sūnzi, "grandson," and sūnnǚ, "granddaughter," include ONLY THE CHILDREN OF ONE'S SON. (The children of one's daughter are called wàisūnzi and wàisūnnǚ.)

Sì Shū: "the Four Books," which are Dàxué, "The Great Learning"; Zhōngyōng, "The Doctrine of the Mean"; Lúnyǔ, "The Analects of Confucius"; and Mèngzǐ, "Mencius." Dàxué and Zhōngyōng are chapters from Lǐ Jì, "The Book of Rites," which were raised to the status of separate "books" by the Southern Sòng Dynasty philosopher Zhū Xī. After the Sòng Dynasty, philosophers of the Idealist school looked upon the Four Books as the classics of Confucianism. Many older Chinese you meet today STUDIED THE FOUR BOOKS when they were children.
